summary: Extends IS-IS to support optimal routing in a domain with two levels. It changes how routes are passed down from one level to the other so that a router can choose the best path, instead of being limited by route summarization between levels. It replaces RFC 2966 and extends the semantics of RFC 1195.

plainLanguage.summary: A big country is split into regions, and normally the regions only share summaries. This lets them share more detail, so travelers can take the truly shortest road rather than a roundabout one.

questions: what is the is-is up down bit
is-is level 1 to level 2 route leaking
subtitle: How IS-IS routers in a two-level network can share detailed prefixes between levels without creating routing loops.

tldr.problem: In a two-level IS-IS network, routers in an area only see summaries of the rest of the domain, so they often pick routes that are not the best ones.
tldr.mechanism: L1L2 routers may advertise more specific IP prefixes between level 1 and level 2 in both directions. An up/down bit marks prefixes that were pushed down from level 2, so they are never advertised back up.
tldr.outcome: Routes can be chosen with more complete information, at the cost of more prefixes, memory and computation throughout the domain. It replaced the Informational RFC 2966 and is on the standards track.

facts.label: Up/down bit
facts.value: High-order bit (bit 8) of the default metric

today: RFC 5302 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2966 and updates RFC 1195. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two-Level IS-IS and Its Limits
sections.content:
An IS-IS routing domain can be split into several level 1 (L1) areas plus a connected level 2 (L2) part of the topology that joins all the areas. Inside an L1 area, routers exchange full link state information. L2 routers exchange L2 link state information to compute routes between areas.

Under RFC 1195, an L1 router that cannot find a destination in its L1 database forwards the packet to the nearest router that is in both L1 and L2 (an L1L2 router) with the attached bit set in its L1 LSP. An L1L2 router is also manually configured with a set of prefixes that summarize its area, and those summaries are injected into L2. RFC 1195 specifies nothing more for IPv4 prefixes.

This RFC extends those semantics so L1 and L2 can exchange IP prefixes in both directions. It replaces the Informational RFC 2966 and states that no other intentional substantive changes were made.
sections.plainLanguage: Each region of a country has a gate city. Normally a traveler who does not know where to go just heads to the nearest gate and hopes for the best. This RFC lets the regions swap better maps.

sections.title: Why Share More Prefixes, and What It Costs
sections.content:
Summarizing loses information, and routes computed from less information are frequently not optimal. If an area has two L1L2 routers that each advertise one summary, a distant L2 router just picks one of them. That router may be the worse choice when seen from inside the area. In the other direction, using the nearest L1L2 router acts like a default route with no metric information.

Two more drivers are named. First, BGP selection depends partly on the IGP cost to the BGP next hop, a technique known as shortest exit routing, which needs exact metrics to BGP speakers in other areas. Second, current practice is to copy the IS-IS metric into the BGP Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED), which only works well if the metric reflects the true distance across the domain.

The RFC is blunt about the price. Domain-wide prefix distribution increases the number of prefixes throughout the domain, so memory, transmission and computation needs grow. It has no effect on the other scalability benefit of areas, which is limiting the spread of the link state database. It is a compromise between scalability and optimality, and normal provisioning guidelines for a fully hierarchical deployment do not apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A short summary is easy to carry but you lose details, like knowing which of two doors is really closer. Sharing more detail finds better routes, but the maps get heavier to carry.

sections.title: The Up/Down Bit and L2 to L1 Routes
sections.content:
RFC 1195 already lets L1L2 routers advertise L1 routes into L2, in the IP Internal Reachability Information TLV (TLV 128). These L1 to L2 inter-area routes look exactly like L2 intra-area routes. RFC 1195 does not define the reverse direction. A simple extension would let an L1L2 router advertise routes it learned through L2 in its L1 LSP, but to prevent loops such routes MUST NOT be advertised back into L2 once they were learned via L1. That requires a way to tell L2 to L1 routes from real L1 intra-area routes.

RFC 5305 defines an up/down bit for this in the extended IP reachability TLV (TLV 135). This RFC redefines the reserved high-order bit (bit 8) of the default metric field in TLVs 128 and 130 as the same up/down bit. L1L2 routers MUST set it to one for prefixes derived from L2 routing and advertised into L1 LSPs, and to zero for all other IP prefixes. Prefixes with the bit set that are learned via L1 MUST NOT be advertised back into L2.

The RFC also loosens RFC 1195 by allowing the IP External Reachability Information TLV (TLV 130) in L1 LSPs. When an L1L2 router passes an externally learned prefix between levels, it SHOULD keep it in TLV 130, and internal prefixes SHOULD stay in TLV 128. Because the advertiser may no longer be the router that first injected the prefix, advertising external routes with external metrics across levels is less useful.
sections.plainLanguage: When a route is sent down from the big highway map to a region, it gets a stamp that says 'came from above'. Gate cities must never send stamped routes back up, which keeps directions from going round in circles.

sections.title: The Types of IP Routes in IS-IS
sections.content:
Four variables describe how an IP prefix is advertised: the level of the LSP (1 or 2), the route-type (internal in TLV 128 or external in TLV 130), the metric-type (internal or external, taken from bit 7 of the metric field), and whether the route has been leaked down the hierarchy (the up/down bit).

The combination of internal reachability with the external metric-type is not allowed, and the up/down bit MUST NOT be set in L2 LSPs. That leaves 8 combinations, but the RFC lists more named route kinds because some are indistinguishable on the wire. For example, L1 to L2 inter-area routes look the same as L2 intra-area routes, and L2 to L1 inter-area routes are advertised in L1 LSPs in TLV 128 with the up/down bit set to one.

The RFC also clarifies that routers MUST give the same preference to routes in TLV 128 and routes in TLV 130 when both use the internal metric-type. External-metric routes MUST get less preference than the same routes with the internal metric-type, regardless of the metric values.
sections.plainLanguage: Each route carries a few small labels: which level it came from, whether it is local or from outside, whether its cost is comparable, and whether it was sent down. Together the labels tell a router how much to trust it.

sections.title: Order of Preference
sections.content:
IS-IS cannot rely on metrics alone, so some route types always win over others. One reason is that inter-area routes can only be advertised with a maximum metric of 63. That value does not mean infinity, as a hop count of 16 does in RIP, because a value for infinity would bring counting-to-infinity behavior between two or more L1L2 routers and hurt stability.

The preference rests on four assumptions. Routes derived from L1 routing beat routes derived from L2 routing. Internal routes and external routes with internal metric-type are equal. External routes with internal metric-type beat those with external metric-type. Routes derived from L2 routing beat L2 to L1 routes.

From these, the RFC gives six ranks, shown below, from most to least preferred.

Implementers are also told that L1L2 routers SHOULD advertise into L2 only the L1 routes they use for forwarding themselves, and SHOULD NOT unconditionally advertise everything in the L1 database. Implementations might allow manual filtering or summarization to cut the number of inter-area prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: When two roads lead to the same place, there is a ranking: local roads first, then roads from the big map, then roads that were sent down, and roads from outside last. Cost only matters among roads of the same rank.

sections.title: Compatibility With Older Routers
sections.content:
The solution is not fully compatible with RFC 1195 but is an extension to it. If routers do not use external L1 routes or L2 to L1 inter-area routes, older implementations that strictly follow RFC 1195 work with newer ones.

Implementations that follow RFC 1195 SHOULD ignore bit 8 of the default metric field, so even older routers can accept L2 to L1 routes. They will install them as L1 intra-area routes, which does not by itself cause loops among L1-only routers. Routers that do not accept TLV 130 in L1 LSPs cannot compute external L1 routes, which could cause loops between L1-only routers that understand them and L1-only routers that use the default route.

The critical point is that L1L2 routers must understand the up/down bit. An old L1L2 router would treat a pushed-down route as an L1 intra-area route and advertise it back into L2, which can cause routing loops, sub-optimal routing or instability. So if L2 routes are advertised into an L1 area, all L1L2 routers in that area must run software that understands the bit. By default, implementations are RECOMMENDED not to advertise any L2 routes into L1, and SHOULD force the administrator to configure this manually.
sections.plainLanguage: Old routers do not know about the stamp. Most can still read the new routes, but the gate cities absolutely must know about the stamp, or routes could circle forever. So the feature starts switched off.

sections.title: Security and Alternatives
sections.content:
The security section is one sentence: the document raises no new security issues for IS-IS, and general IS-IS security considerations are in RFC 5304.

The RFC also compares itself with RFC 5305, whose new TLVs also carry an up/down bit and have a wider metric space, giving more granular inter-area path costs. To use that wider space fully, administrators must deploy both new TLVs at the same time, which requires upgrading all routers in the network. The approach in this document needs only an upgrade of the L1L2 routers in selected areas, so it might be a good alternative when a network-wide upgrade is hard.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is risky here. If you want a bigger upgrade with finer detail, there is another RFC, but it means changing every router. This one only needs the gate cities changed.
